SMTO-FIL-0055 — SMTO can't save there because the drive is read-only

GUID: 4d65c665-4582-41f7-aa7c-95bea802b4b4
Slug: file-read-only-filesystem
Domain: FIL · Subsystem: fil

What happened

  • The computer doesn't allow any changes on that drive or folder because it is set to read-only, so SMTO couldn't save there.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. If it's a USB stick or memory card, look for a small lock switch on its side, slide it to unlocked, and plug it back in. A locked switch makes the whole drive read-only.
  2. Otherwise, tell SMTO to save to a different folder you know you can change, such as one on the computer's own disk. SMTO won't pick a new destination by itself, so you need to name it.
  3. If you must use that drive, ask the person who manages that computer to make it writable again. Read-only drives are set by the computer itself; changing a file's permissions can't undo it.

What success looks like

  • SMTO saves the file and it appears in the destination folder.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO or that computer. Before trying again, ask SMTO to list the destination so you know whether any files were already saved.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The target filesystem rejected a write with EROFS (or Windows ERROR_WRITE_PROTECT) because it is mounted or configured read-only.

What this means

  • The OS returned EROFS or Windows write-protect status for a requested filesystem change. File and transfer receipts retain per-item execution, publication, cleanup and partial-effect facts. These explanations do not modify files, weaken path guards or replay a write; reconcile the original state before further mutation.

Why this can happen

  • The OS returned EROFS or Windows write-protect status for a requested filesystem change.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect mount/media write-protection state rather than assuming ordinary file mode bits are the cause.

How to fix it

  • Check the target's mount options (findmnt or mount on Linux, or the media's write-protect status on Windows). Remount read-write if authorized, clear hardware write protection, or select another writable destination; changing file modes cannot make a read-only filesystem writable.
  • Choose an authorized writable destination or ask the host administrator to repair the mount state. File mode changes alone cannot make a read-only filesystem writable.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The intended authorized destination is writable under its accepted mount/media policy.

What not to do

  • Do not silently substitute a different target for a saved run or move its existing execution authority.

Technical notes

  • File and transfer receipts retain per-item execution, publication, cleanup and partial-effect facts. These explanations do not modify files, weaken path guards or replay a write; reconcile the original state before further mutation.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
